channel.title: Applied Inference Weekly
channel.description: Long-form engineering writing on serving models in production.

item.title: What Actually Broke When We Doubled Context
item.author: R. Engineer
item.description:
We moved from a 200k window to a 1M window expecting a capacity problem and got a scheduling problem instead. This post walks through the three things that actually degraded, with the traces that showed them.

The first was prefill. At 200k our prefill was comfortably inside the budget we had allocated per request, so batching decisions were dominated by decode. At 1M the prefill cost for a single long request could exceed the decode cost of an entire batch of short ones, which meant our scheduler — which had been assuming roughly uniform request cost — started making choices that were locally reasonable and globally terrible. A single long-context request would arrive, claim a slot, and stall a dozen short requests behind it.

The second was the KV cache. Doubling the window more than doubled our working set, because the requests that use long context are also the requests that get retried and continued. We were evicting cache entries that we were about to need again, and the eviction policy had no notion of that.

The third was our own instrumentation. Our p99 latency metric was computed per request without normalising for input length, so the number went up and told us almost nothing about why. Splitting the metric by input-length bucket was the change that made the other two problems visible, and in hindsight it should have been the first thing we did rather than the last.

The fix for the scheduler was to price a request by estimated total tokens rather than by request count, which is obvious in retrospect and was not obvious at the time. We have included the before-and-after queue depth graphs below.

item.title: A Cheaper Eval Harness That Still Catches Regressions
item.author: R. Engineer
item.description:
Our eval suite cost more per month than the service it was testing. Here is how we cut it by roughly 80% without losing the regressions we care about.

The starting observation was that most of our eval cases were testing the same handful of behaviours through slightly different wording. That redundancy felt like rigour and was actually just cost: when a regression appeared, forty cases failed together, and the forty-first told us nothing the first one hadn't. We clustered the suite by which behaviour each case exercised and kept the cheapest representative of each cluster, plus every case that had ever been the sole detector of a real regression.

The second change was to stop running the full suite on every commit. We split it into a fast tier that runs on every change and a full tier that runs nightly and before a release. The fast tier is chosen to maximise the chance of catching a regression at all, not to characterise it precisely — that is the nightly tier's job.

The third change was the least popular internally and had the largest effect: we deleted every eval whose pass criterion was a model judging free text without a rubric. Those cases were noisy enough that people had learned to ignore their failures, which is worse than not having them.

item.title: Notes On Running Two Model Versions Side By Side
item.author: R. Engineer
item.description:
Version pinning sounds like a configuration detail until you are serving two versions at once and discover your caches, metrics, and prompt templates all quietly assumed there was only one.

Prompt caches are per-model, so a naive rollout halves your cache hit rate at exactly the moment you are watching latency most closely. We staged the rollout by cohort rather than by percentage so that each cohort's cache stayed warm, and accepted a slower rollout in exchange for a readable latency graph.

Metrics needed a model-version dimension added everywhere, including in the dashboards we had not touched in a year. The ones we forgot showed up as inexplicable step changes that took an afternoon each to trace back.

The thing we got right by accident: our prompt templates were already in version control with the model id in the path, so nothing silently reused a prompt tuned for the old version. That was a decision someone made two years ago for unrelated reasons and it saved us a week.
